newsitem.title: MALTA: Europe puts foot in door of Mideast diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Europe puts foot in door of Mideast diplomacy.

text.p: Europe has put its foot in the door as a mediator in the Arab-Israeli conflict, pulling off a surprise diplomatic coup at a meeting of European and Mediterranean foreign ministers in Malta.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo brought Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy together on Wednesday on the sidelines of the conference.
For years the absence of "the European role" has been the lament of the Arab world. Now that role has a little substance, if only as a carbon copy of the well-known U.S. version.
Van Mierlo, whose country is president of the European Union, crowed with delight that the Euro-Mediterranean forum had given Europe a stage on which to flex its muscles.

"It's indispensable, the political role of Europe here. I knew that but sometimes it's nice that you get the instrument to make it also clear to others and that's what happened today and yesterday," he told the closing news conference.
Europe has long complained that its ability to sway the course of Middle East peace talks does not match its significance as a trading partner and aid donor.
The unspoken target of these jibes is the United States, which has tended to monopolise the role of mediator through its global power and its close alliance with the Jewish state.
Back in the 1970s late Egyptian President Anwar Sadat liked to say that Washington held 99 percent of the cards in the Middle East. For him at least, Europe did not count.
Israel and the United States have poured cold water on previous European attempts to elbow in on Washington's act, Israel sometimes with brutal frankness.
The latest direct rebuff came last month when the United States vetoed a European-sponsored U.N. Security Council resolution critical of Israel's settlement policy.
Israel said the resolution harmed European attempts to mediate between it and the Palestinians.

"The expectation of the Palestinians and the Arab world that Europe will always stand behind every claim and violation of theirs...is one of the obstacles that prevent us from moving forward," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Europeans have also failed to satisfy the Arab side, which would like them to take their opposition to Jewish settlements beyond mere rhetoric.

The turn of events at the conference in Malta showed that, far from breaking new ground in Middle East diplomacy, the Europeans achieved their ends mainly by adopting the same U.S. methods that have long alienated Arab public opinion.
U.S. diplomats believe in the intrinsic and absolute virtue of dialogue between Israelis and Palestinians, regardless of what the Israelis do to the Palestinians on the ground.
The Palestinians say this attitude merely encourages the Israelis to play for time in the negotiations while grabbing more Palestinian land by force of arms.
Arafat had been reluctant to meet Levy without receiving a political gesture in return, especially on the Jewish settlement that Israel is building in disputed East Jerusalem.
The Israelis offered him nothing but more talks and Levy said later that Arafat had agreed to resume security cooperation against Palestinians who attack Israelis.

Van Mierlo recognised on Wednesday the limits of the European accomplishment. "We have not yet achieved specific results but we didn't actually expect that. But we have achieved something which was yesterday evening thought impossible. They were able to meet and talk," he said.
For the Arabs, this photo-opportunity mediation is a type they don't much need, though they are reluctant to say so in public because they hope for more from Europe in the future.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, asked if Europe was playing its role, indicated he was still a sceptic.
"It depends on the Europeans if they want to play a role. We believe they can play a role because of the relations they have with the Arab side and with Israel," he said.
"But any European role has to be based on the (European) position statements," he added.
In other words, the Europeans should press Israel to meet Europe's criteria for a settlement, such as "land for peace" and Palestinian self-determination.
When the Europeans do try that, the Israelis just brush them aside. "The question, as always, is whether the Israelis are ready to listen to us," said one European delegate.
